lines.text: Ratings, Herding and Price Discovery on a
Sequential Platform: A Long Fixture
Anonymous
Abstract
We study how buyers on a sequential platform learn from the rat-
ings left by earlier buyers. A staggered change in how ratings are
displayed lets us compare markets before and after the change. Dis-
playing the full distribution of ratings, rather than the mean alone,
raises the share of buyers who act on their own information. The ef-
fect is statistically significant but economically small, and it fades in
markets with many sellers. We interpret the evidence through a model
of observational learning in which the display rule controls how much
of the history each buyer can read.
1 Introduction
Buyers on online platforms rarely see the product before they pay for it.
What they see instead is a record of what earlier buyers did and said. A
large literature treats such records as a channel of observational learning, in
which each agent combines a private signal with the actions of predecessors
(Banerjee,1992;Bikhchandanietal.,1992). Whenthepublicrecordbecomes
informative enough, agents stop using their own signals and an information
cascade begins. The record then stops improving, because no later action
reveals anything new. This paper asks whether the way a platform displays
its record changes how quickly buyers fall into such a cascade.

We exploit a change in the display rule of an anonymised marketplace
for used equipment. Over eighteen months the platform replaced the mean
ratingwithahistogramofratings, oneproductcategoryatatime, inanorder
that was fixed in advance for reasons unrelated to demand. The staggered
rollout gives us treated and not-yet-treated categories in every month of the
sample. Our main outcome is the share of buyers whose purchase decision
departs from the majority of the decisions displayed to them, a measure of
how often buyers act on their own information.
Three findings stand out. First, the histogram raises the share of buyers
who depart from the displayed majority by 2.4 percentage points, against
a pre-rollout mean of 11.8 percent. Second, the effect is concentrated in
categories with few sellers; in categories with more than forty active sellers
it is indistinguishable from zero. Third, prices move more after a negative
rating once the histogram is shown, which suggests that sellers respond to
the information buyers now read. Taken together, the results indicate that
the display rule matters for learning, but less than the literature on cascades
might lead one to expect.
2 Institutional background
The marketplace began as a bulletin board on which laboratories sold surplus
instruments to one another. It became a platform with posted prices, pay-
ments held in escrow and a rating system about a decade before our sample
begins. Sellers list items one at a time, and most listings are unique: a par-
ticular centrifuge with a particular history of use. Buyers therefore cannot
learn about the item from other buyers of the same item, only from other
buyers of the same seller. The rating record attached to a listing is the record
of the seller, and it accumulates across all of that seller’s listings.
Ratings take five levels, from one to five stars, and a buyer may rate
a purchase only after the escrow period has ended. Before the change we
study, the product page showed the mean of the seller’s ratings rounded to

Neither display showed the text of reviews on the product page; the text was
one click away on the seller’s profile, and the platform’s logs show that fewer

The platform charges a commission on each sale and earns nothing from

to reduce disputes over items that did not match their description, which
had risen in the year before the rollout. Disputes are costly for the plat-

with divided records could reduce disputes even if it reduced sales, and the
platform appears to have accepted that trade-off.
3 Related literature
ThetheoryofobservationallearningbeginswithBanerjee(1992)andBikhchan-
dani et al. (1992), who show that rational agents who observe only the ac-
tions of predecessors can herd on the wrong action with positive probability.
Smith and Sørensen (2000) show that the result depends on the strength
of private signals: with unbounded signals, learning is eventually complete,
while bounded signals allow cascades that never break. Acemoglu et al.
(2011) extend the analysis to agents who observe only some predecessors
and characterise the network structures under which learning is asymptoti-
cally efficient. Our display rule can be read as a change in the observation
structure that these papers study.
A second strand studies markets in which prices respond to the history
of trades. Avery and Zemsky (1998) show that a market maker who updates
prices after each trade can prevent herding when there is a single dimension
of uncertainty, but that herding returns when traders are uncertain about
more than one dimension of the asset. The platform we study has posted
prices set by sellers rather than a market maker, yet sellers revise prices after
ratings arrive, and the question of whether price adjustment undoes herding
arises in a similar form. Kogan (2020) studies learning from reviews when
sellers act strategically, and Lee (2021) studies observational learning when
buyers hold heterogeneous priors. Both mechanisms appear in our setting.
A third strand concerns the procedures through which a sequence of
agents aggregates information. Dekel and Piccione (2000) compare sequen-
tial and simultaneous voting in symmetric binary elections and show that

4 Model
A sequence of buyers t= 1,2,... arrives at a product page. The product is
of high quality with prior probability π and of low quality otherwise. Each
buyer receives a private signal st whose distribution depends on the quality,
and observes a public display dt that summarises the decisions and ratings of
earlier buyers. Buyer tpurchases when her posterior belief that the product
is of high quality exceeds a threshold cthat reflects the price and her outside
option. After purchasing she leaves a rating that is informative about quality
but noisy.
The display rule determines what dt contains. Under the mean rule, dt
is the average rating among earlier purchasers together with their number.
Under the histogram rule, dt is the count of each rating level. The posterior
belief of buyer t satisfies

lines.text: the model a variant of the standard sequential learning model with a selected
public history.
We make two assumptions that keep the analysis tractable. First, private
signals are bounded, so that there exist public histories after which no private
signal can overturn the public belief. Second, the price is fixed within a spell
of the page and is revised by the seller only between spells. The second
assumption is restrictive, and we relax it in the empirical work by allowing
prices to respond to ratings with a lag.
4.1 Ratings and selection
Ratings are informative only about the buyers who chose to purchase. To
see what this implies, consider a seller whose items are of high quality with
probability one half. If the first two buyers draw favourable signals and
purchase, both leave ratings, and the third buyer sees two ratings drawn from
thepopulationofpurchasers. Ifinsteadthefirstbuyerdrawsanunfavourable
signal and declines, the record stays empty, and the second buyer faces the
prior alone. The record is thus a censored sample of experiences, and its
informativeness depends on the history of decisions as much as on the quality
of the item.
The histogram changes the censoring problem in one respect. Under the
mean rule a buyer cannot tell a record of uniformly mediocre ratings from a
record that mixes delight and disappointment. Under the histogram rule she
can, and the second kind of record is far more likely when purchasers differ
in how well the item suits them. The model captures this through a match
component in each purchaser’s experience, so that ratings vary even for a
seller whose quality is known. The variance of ratings is then informative
about the importance of match, and only the histogram reveals it.
5 Equilibrium

itive probability, and that the probability of a cascade on the wrong action is
lower under the histogram rule. The intuition is that the histogram reveals
disagreement among earlier purchasers. A product whose ratings are split
between the highest and the lowest levels has the same mean as a product
whose ratings are all in the middle, yet the two histories have different like-

5

lines.text: lihoods under high and low quality. A buyer who sees the split knows that
the public belief is less certain than the mean suggests, and her own signal
regains weight.
The proof follows the argument of Bikhchandani et al. (1992) with minor
modifications. It is easy to see that the inequality is preserved when both
sides are multiplied by the likelihood ratio of the display. Because the his-
togram rule refines the mean rule, every history that starts a cascade under
the histogram rule also starts one under the mean rule, while the converse
fails for histories with dispersed ratings. The set of histories that start a
cascade is therefore smaller under the histogram rule.
Proposition 2 concerns the number of sellers. When several sellers offer
close substitutes, a buyer who declines one product often purchases another,
and her rating then informs the record of the second product. Competition
among sellers thus spreads information across pages and weakens the link
between any single display and the decision of any single buyer. The model
predicts that the effect of the display rule falls with the number of active
sellers in a category, a prediction we take to the data in the section on
heterogeneity.
5.1 Comparative statics
Two comparative statics guide the empirical work. First, the effect of the
display rule on the probability of a cascade is larger when private signals are
less precise. With precise signals, buyers seldom defer to the record under
either rule, and a finer record changes few decisions. With imprecise signals,
the record carries most of the weight, and a record that reveals disagreement
can restore the weight of private information for many buyers. We measure
signal precision by how often buyers ask sellers questions before purchasing.
Second, the effect falls as the number of substitutes rises. When a buyer
can choose among many sellers of similar items, her decision at any one page
is less consequential, and the information she reveals by declining is spread
thinlyacrossalternatives. Themodelthereforepredictsthesmallesteffectsin
the densest categories. A third prediction, that the effect should be larger for
sellers with more ratings, follows because the histogram and the mean differ
more when there are more ratings to summarise; we find mixed support for
it.

lines.text: 6 Data
The data come from an anonymised marketplace for used laboratory and
workshop equipment. Sellers are small firms and individuals; buyers are
firms, universities and hobbyists. Each listing has a product page with a de-
scription, photographs, a posted price and the rating record of earlier buyers
of the same seller. A buyer can message the seller before purchasing, and
about a third of purchases follow such a message. We observe every page
visit, every purchase and every rating between the first month of the sample
and the twenty-fourth.
Our unit of observation is a visit by a registered buyer to a product page.
Wekeepvisitsbybuyerswhohadnotpurchasedfromthesellerbefore,sothat
the rating record is the main source of public information. We drop pages
with fewer than three ratings, for which the two display rules are almost
identical, and pages whose seller changed the price during the visit. The
resulting sample contains 1.9 million visits to 214,000 pages in 46 product
categories. The median page has eleven ratings at the time of the visit, and
the median category has 27 active sellers.
The outcome we focus on is whether the visit ends in a decision that
departsfromthemajorityofthedecisionsdisplayed. Apurchasedepartsfrom
the majority when most earlier visitors whose decisions the display reveals
did not purchase, and a decision not to purchase departs from the majority
in the opposite case. Because the display reveals decisions only through
ratings, we construct the majority from the ratings and the count of visits
that the platform records internally, which buyers cannot see. The measure
is therefore defined from information the buyer could not fully observe, which
biases our estimates toward zero if anything.
6.1 Descriptive statistics
Before the rollout, 64 percent of visits to a page with at least three ratings
ended without a purchase, and 11.8 percent of visits ended in a decision that
departed from the displayed majority. Departures were more common on
pages whose mean rating was between three and four stars, where the record
is least decisive, and least common on pages with a mean above four and a
half. The share of departures also fell with the number of ratings, from 15
percent on pages with three to five ratings to 8 percent on pages with more
than fifty.

lines.text: Prices are posted by sellers and revised infrequently: the median listing
changes its price once during its life on the platform. Price revisions cluster
in the two days after a new rating arrives, and about two thirds of revisions
after a rating of one or two stars are reductions. Sellers with many listings
revise prices more often than sellers with few, which suggests that revising
is costly in attention and that large sellers have routines for it.
7 Empirical strategy
Our identification strategy exploits the staggered rollout of the histogram
display. The platform introduced the histogram in two or three categories at
a time, following a schedule set at the start of the project by the engineering
team, which ordered categories by the size of their page templates. Internal
documents describe the schedule as a matter of software maintenance. We
verify that categories treated early and late do not differ in pre-rollout trends
of purchases, ratings or prices.
We estimate event-study regressions of the departure indicator on leads
and lags of the rollout date, with category and month fixed effects and con-
trols for the number of ratings displayed. Because treatment effects may vary
across cohorts, we use an estimator that compares each treated cohort only
with categories not yet treated. Standard errors are clustered by category.
With 46 categories the number of clusters is modest, and we report wild
bootstrap confidence intervals alongside conventional ones.
The main threat to identification is that the platform changed something
else at the same time as the display. Two changes coincided with parts of
the rollout: a redesign of the search page and a new policy on returns. The
search redesign was introduced in all categories at once and is absorbed by
the month fixed effects. The returns policy applied to a subset of sellers,
and we show that the results are unchanged when we drop the categories in
which those sellers are active.
7.1 Event-study evidence
The event-study coefficients trace the path of the effect around the rollout.
In the six months before the rollout the coefficients fluctuate around zero,
with no trend and no single coefficient larger than half a percentage point
in absolute value. The effect appears in the first month after the rollout,

else at the same time as the display. Two changes coincided with parts of
the rollout: a redesign of the search page and a new policy on returns. The
search redesign was introduced in all categories at once and is absorbed by
the month fixed effects. The returns policy applied to a subset of sellers,
and we show that the results are unchanged when we drop the categories in
which those sellers are active.
7.1 Event-study evidence
The event-study coefficients trace the path of the effect around the rollout.
In the six months before the rollout the coefficients fluctuate around zero,
with no trend and no single coefficient larger than half a percentage point
in absolute value. The effect appears in the first month after the rollout,
8

lines.text: reaches its full size by the third month and remains stable thereafter. The
gradual onset is consistent with buyers learning to read the new display, and
with the record of each page filling up with ratings left by buyers who saw
the histogram.
We also estimatethe eventstudyseparately forcohorts treated in thefirst
and second halves of the rollout. The two paths are similar, which suggests
that the effect did not depend on the season in which a category was treated
or on what buyers had learnt from the categories treated earlier. A test of
equal post-rollout coefficients across cohorts does not reject at conventional
levels.

10

lines.text: than fifteen active sellers the estimate is 0.041, while in categories with more
than forty it is 0.003 with a standard error of 0.006. This pattern matches
Proposition 2. With many sellers, a buyer who is unconvinced by one page
moves to another, and the display of any single page matters less for her
final decision. The finding cautions against extrapolating the average effect
to markets with dense competition.
10 Mechanisms
Three mechanisms could produce the main result: better information about
quality, better information about match, and greater salience of the ratings.
The model emphasises the first two, which we try to separate by looking at
returns. A buyer who departs from a favourable majority because she infers
poor quality should avoid the item altogether, while a buyer who departs
because she infers poor match should look for a similar item from another
seller. The data favour the match channel: most buyers who decline a page
with a divided record purchase a similar item within a week.
Salience is harder to rule out, because any display that adds information
also changes how the page looks. The design change discussed in the section
on robustness, which enlarged the mean rating without adding information,
offers one test, and it suggests that salience alone does not move decisions.
A second test uses buyers who visit a page more than once. If the histogram
worked through salience, its effect should be largest on the first visit and fade
on later ones; instead the effect is similar on first and repeat visits.
Seller responses form a fourth channel. If sellers with divided records
lower their prices after the rollout, some buyers who would otherwise depart
from a favourable majority may purchase at the lower price. Price responses
therefore dampen the measured effect on departures, and the estimates in
Table 1 combine the direct effect of the display with the indirect effect of
prices. A model-based decomposition attributes about a fifth of the direct
effect to offsetting price changes.

11 Robustness
We examine five threats to the interpretation of the main estimate. First, the
composition of buyers might have changed with the rollout, for example if the
11

lines.text: histogramattractedmoreexperiencedbuyers. Wefindnochangeintheshare
of first-time buyers or in the distribution of buyer tenure around the rollout
dates. Second, sellers might have responded by changing the descriptions or
photographs on their pages. A text comparison of descriptions before and
after the rollout shows no systematic change, and the results are unchanged
when we restrict the sample to pages whose description did not change.
Third, the departure measure might be mechanically related to the num-
ber of ratings, since pages with more ratings have more stable majorities.
We control flexibly for the number of ratings and obtain the same estimates;
the results also hold within bins of the rating count. Fourth, the platform’s
internal visit counts might be measured with error. We repeat the analy-
sis with a majority defined from ratings alone and find a smaller but still
significant effect, as expected if the measurement error is classical.
Fifth, we consider whether the effect reflects attention rather than infor-
mation. A histogram occupies more space on the page than a single number,
so buyers might simply notice the ratings more often. To separate the two
channels we use a design change that enlarged the mean rating in some cat-
egories without adding information. The enlargement had no effect on de-
partures, which suggests that the histogram works through the information
it adds and not through its size on the screen.
A final robustness check concerns the timing of the rollout within each
month. The platform deployed each change on a Tuesday, and visits early
in the week differ from visits at the weekend in the mix of buyers. Defining
treatmentbytheexactdeploymentdateratherthanbycalendarmonthleaves
the estimates unchanged. We also obtain similar results when we drop the
month of the rollout entirely, which removes visits that saw both displays.
We have also checked that the results do not depend on the definition of
a product category. The platform’s own categories are broad, and some con-
tain items as different as microscopes and soldering stations. Re-estimating
with finer categories constructed from listing titles gives an estimate of 0.022
with a slightly wider interval. Results are similar when we weight categories
equally rather than by the number of visits.

lines.text: the rating the buyer leaves and by whether she returns the product. Buyers
who depart from the majority under the histogram display leave higher rat-
ings and return products less often than buyers who depart under the mean
display, which indicates that the additional departures are informed rather
thanrandom. Aback-of-the-envelopecalculationsuggeststhatthehistogram
reduces the share of purchases that end in a return by 0.4 percentage points.
The gains are not evenly shared. Sellers with polarised records lose sales
under the histogram display, while sellers whose ratings cluster near the
mean gain. Because polarised records are more common among new sellers,
the histogram may make entry harder. We find that the number of new
sellers in treated categories falls by about three percent in the six months
after the rollout, although the estimate is imprecise.
13 External validity
How far do the results travel? Three features of the setting are unusual.
Items are unique, so the record describes the seller rather than the item;
buyers are often professionals; and prices are posted rather than negotiated.
On platforms where many buyers purchase the same item, the record de-
scribes the item directly, and a histogram may matter more because ratings
accumulate faster. On platforms where buyers are consumers with weaker
private information, the model predicts larger effects, since the record then
carries more weight.
Themodestaverageeffectshouldalsobereadagainstthebackgroundofa
mature platform. Buyers in our sample had seen thousands of rating displays
before the change and had formed habits of reading them. A platform that
introducedahistogramfromitsstartmightfindlargereffects, becausebuyers
would never have learnt to discount the mean. Conversely, the effects we
measure in the months after the rollout may overstate the long-run effect if
buyers eventually learn to read the histogram as they had learnt to read the
mean.

14 Discussion and limitations
Our setting has features that limit how far the results generalise. The mar-
ketplace sells durable equipment to buyers who are often professionals, and
13

lines.text: such buyers may rely on private information more than consumers buying
inexpensive goods. The display rule we study is also only one of many design
choices; platforms vary in whether they show the text of reviews, the identity
of reviewers and the dates of ratings. Each of these choices changes what a
buyer can learn from the record, and the interactions among them are not
identified by our design.
A further limitation concerns the model. We assume that buyers are
sophisticated about the selection of ratings, but evidence from other settings
suggests that many buyers take ratings at face value. If buyers are naive, the
histogram may help them by making the dispersion of opinions visible, even
if it adds nothing for a sophisticated buyer. Distinguishing between these
interpretations would require data on beliefs, which we do not have.
15 Extensions of the model
The model can be extended in two directions that the data suggest. First,
buyers may differ in how much they read. Some read only the summary,
while others open the seller’s profile and read the text of reviews. A mixture
of the two types predicts that the histogram matters most for buyers who
read little, since buyers who read the text already know when opinions are
divided. Our data on profile visits are consistent with this prediction: the
effect is concentrated among buyers who never open a seller’s profile.
Second, sellersmaychoosewhichitemstolistinresponsetotherecord. A
seller whose record is divided might specialise in items for which match mat-
ters less, so as to attract buyers whose experiences are more uniform. Over
a longer horizon than our sample, this response could reduce the dispersion
of ratings and with it the information the histogram adds. Studying such
responses would require following sellers for several years after the change.
Athirdextensionconcernstheplatform’schoiceofdisplay. Iftheplatform
cares about disputes and commissions, it faces a trade-off between informing
buyers and maximising sales, and the optimal display may reveal some but
not all of the history. Characterising that optimum is beyond the scope of
this paper, but the estimates here provide the elasticities such an analysis
would need.

lines.text: 16 Conclusion
Displaying the distribution of ratings rather than their mean makes buyers
on a sequential platform act on their own information somewhat more often.
The effect is clearly present but small, it is concentrated in thin markets,
and it is accompanied by faster price responses to bad news. These findings
supporttheviewthattheobservationstructureshapeslearningonplatforms,
while suggesting that most buyers in most markets are far from the cascades
that dominate the theory. Future work could combine display experiments
with direct measures of beliefs to separate the information a display adds
from the attention it draws.
